title: Multi-Table Inner Join with Aliasing & Foreign Key Traversal
whatThisCodeCovers: Traverses a normalized 3-tier relational schema (customers -> orders -> order_items -> products) to aggregate customer purchases without data duplication.
code:
-- Querying customer order lines across normalized relational boundaries
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.full_name,
    o.order_id,
    o.order_date,
    p.product_name,
    oi.quantity,
    oi.unit_price,
    (oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS line_total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o 
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
INNER JOIN order_items oi 
    ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
INNER JOIN products p 
    ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE o.order_status = 'COMPLETED'
  AND o.order_date >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, oi.item_id ASC;
breakdown: Uses ANSI explicit INNER JOIN syntax with clear ON predicates instead of legacy comma-joins in WHERE.
Traverses foreign keys from customers down to line items and dimension products in logical order.
Performs inline arithmetic (quantity * unit_price) on projection without modifying base relations.
Applies deterministic multi-column sorting (order_date DESC, item_id ASC).
expectedOutput:
customer_id | full_name   | order_id | order_date | product_name   | quantity | unit_price | line_total
101         | Alice Smith | 5001     | 2026-02-15 | PostgreSQL Pro | 2        | 49.99      | 99.98
102         | Bob Jones   | 5002     | 2026-02-14 | ANSI SQL Guide | 1        | 39.50      | 39.50

title: Left Outer Join with IS NULL Filter for Unmatched Records (Anti-Join Pattern)
whatThisCodeCovers: Detects dormant or orphan records by preserving all left-table rows and filtering for NULLs generated on the unmatched right side.
code:
-- Find all registered customers who have never placed a single order
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.email,
    c.registered_at
FROM customers c
LEFT OUTER JOIN orders o 
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
breakdown: LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves every row from customers, populating order columns with NULL if no match exists.
The WHERE o.order_id IS NULL clause filters out any customer who had matching orders.
Testing the right table's primary key (order_id) guarantees NULL means 'no record found', not an optional attribute with NULL.
A classic relational difference pattern implemented via join mechanics.
expectedOutput:
customer_id | email               | registered_at
204         | inactive@acme.com   | 2025-11-10 09:12:00
319         | newuser@domain.org  | 2026-01-04 14:30:22

title: High-Performance Anti-Join using NOT EXISTS vs NOT IN with Nullable Columns
whatThisCodeCovers: Demonstrates safe relational exclusion using NOT EXISTS to avoid the three-valued logic (3VL) trap where NOT IN with a single NULL yields zero rows.
code:
-- Safe and high-performance search for departments without active staff
-- (NOT IN (SELECT ...) would return 0 rows if any employee had department_id IS NULL)
SELECT 
    d.department_id,
    d.department_name
FROM departments d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 
    FROM employees e 
    WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id
);
breakdown: NOT EXISTS evaluates whether the correlated inner query returns at least one row, terminating immediately upon first match (short-circuit).
Immune to NULLs: Even if employees contains NULL department_id rows, NOT EXISTS evaluates accurately based on boolean existence.
SELECT 1 inside the subquery emphasizes that no actual columns need to be projected from the inner table.
The optimizer transforms this correlated subquery into an optimized hash anti-join or merge anti-join.
expectedOutput:
department_id | department_name
14            | Research & Exploration
22            | Strategic Acquisitions

title: Semi-Join Pattern with EXISTS for Conditional Parent Selection
whatThisCodeCovers: Uses a semi-join via EXISTS to filter parent entities based on child attributes without duplicating parent rows or requiring costly DISTINCT operations.
code:
-- Find all customers who have placed at least one high-value order (> $1000)
-- Retaining exact 1-to-1 customer cardinality without using DISTINCT
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.full_name,
    c.tier
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND o.total_amount > 1000.00
);
breakdown: If solved with INNER JOIN, customers with 5 high-value orders would appear 5 times, requiring a wasteful DISTINCT.
EXISTS implements relational semi-join semantics: it preserves the exact row set of the left table without row expansion.
Stops scanning child records as soon as one order with total_amount > 1000 is encountered for that customer.
Preserves index seeks on (customer_id, total_amount).
expectedOutput:
customer_id | full_name     | tier
101         | Global Tech   | ENTERPRISE
108         | Apex Logistics| VIP

title: Full Outer Join with COALESCE for Symmetrical Discrepancy Auditing
whatThisCodeCovers: Performs full reconciliation between an internal ledger and an external bank statement, identifying matching records, missing bank deposits, and missing internal entries.
code:
-- Symmetrical financial ledger reconciliation
SELECT 
    COALESCE(l.transaction_ref, b.transaction_ref) AS transaction_ref,
    l.amount AS ledger_amount,
    b.amount AS bank_amount,
    CASE 
        WHEN l.transaction_ref IS NOT NULL AND b.transaction_ref IS NOT NULL THEN 'MATCHED'
        WHEN l.transaction_ref IS NOT NULL AND b.transaction_ref IS NULL THEN 'MISSING_IN_BANK'
        ELSE 'MISSING_IN_LEDGER'
    END AS reconciliation_status
FROM internal_ledger l
FULL OUTER JOIN bank_statement b 
    ON l.transaction_ref = b.transaction_ref
WHERE l.transaction_ref IS NULL 
   OR b.transaction_ref IS NULL 
   OR l.amount <> b.amount;
breakdown: FULL OUTER JOIN retains all rows from both tables, pairing matches and padding missing entries with NULL.
COALESCE ensures that whichever side supplied the transaction_ref is projected cleanly.
A CASE expression classifies each record into matched, missing-in-bank, or missing-in-ledger states.
Filtering for mismatches or amount discrepancies extracts the exact audit discrepancy report.
expectedOutput:
transaction_ref | ledger_amount | bank_amount | reconciliation_status
TXN-901         | 450.00        | NULL        | MISSING_IN_BANK
TXN-902         | NULL          | 1200.00     | MISSING_IN_LEDGER
TXN-903         | 100.00        | 95.00       | MATCHED

title: Self-Join for Hierarchical Parent-Child Lookups Without CTEs
whatThisCodeCovers: Joins an employee table to itself on manager_id = employee_id to retrieve employees alongside their immediate supervisor's details.

ORDER BY e.manager_id NULLS FIRST, e.employee_id;

title: Non-Equi Join for Historical Date-Range & Currency Exchange Rate Matching
whatThisCodeCovers: Joins sales transactions to an effective-dated currency rate dimension using inequality operators (BETWEEN) to accurately convert amounts to USD.
code:
-- Join international orders with historical daily currency conversion rates
SELECT 
    o.order_id,
    o.order_date,
    o.currency_code,
    o.local_amount,
    r.exchange_rate_to_usd,
    ROUND(o.local_amount * r.exchange_rate_to_usd, 2) AS amount_usd
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN currency_rates r 
    ON o.currency_code = r.currency_code
   AND o.order_date BETWEEN r.effective_from AND r.effective_to
WHERE o.currency_code <> 'USD';
breakdown: Unlike equi-joins that compare with '=' non-equi joins use range boundaries like BETWEEN.
Matches the exact currency rate record whose effective date span covers the transaction's order_date.
Enforces temporal consistency without mutating historic order records when exchange rates change.
Rounds resulting financial values to 2 decimal places per standard accounting guidelines.
expectedOutput:
order_id | order_date | currency_code | local_amount | exchange_rate_to_usd | amount_usd

8802     | 2026-03-02 | JPY           | 15000.00     | 0.0067               | 100.50

title: Cross Join for Dimension Matrix Cartesian Expansion (Grid Generation)
whatThisCodeCovers: Constructs a full reporting grid (all branches cross all calendar quarters) combined with a LEFT JOIN to ensure quarters with zero sales are reported as 0 rather than omitted.
code:
-- Dense quarterly sales grid across all retail branches
WITH branch_quarters AS (
    SELECT 
        b.branch_id,
        b.branch_name,
        q.quarter_name,
        q.start_date,
        q.end_date
    FROM branches b
    CROSS JOIN fiscal_quarters q
)
SELECT 
    bq.branch_name,
    bq.quarter_name,
    COALESCE(SUM(s.sale_amount), 0.00) AS total_revenue
FROM branch_quarters bq
LEFT OUTER JOIN sales s 
    ON bq.branch_id = s.branch_id
   AND s.sale_date BETWEEN bq.start_date AND bq.end_date
GROUP BY bq.branch_name, bq.quarter_name
ORDER BY bq.branch_name, bq.quarter_name;
breakdown: CROSS JOIN generates the Cartesian product of M branches and N quarters (M * N dimension cells).
LEFT OUTER JOIN attaches actual sales figures to the Cartesian grid.
COALESCE(SUM(...), 0.00) ensures branches with no sales in a given quarter yield a clear 0.00 instead of vanishing from reports.
Standard pattern for financial and BI reporting dashboards requiring zero-filled timelines.
expectedOutput:
branch_name | quarter_name | total_revenue
Downtown    | 2026-Q1      | 245000.00
Downtown    | 2026-Q2      | 0.00
Uptown      | 2026-Q1      | 185000.00

title: Set Operations: UNION ALL vs UNION Deduplication Performance Benchmark
whatThisCodeCovers: Demonstrates when to use UNION ALL (fast concatenation without sort-unique overhead) versus UNION (strict mathematical set deduplication).
code:
-- 1. UNION ALL: Concatenate archive and active tables without expensive deduplication
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, 'ACTIVE' AS source
FROM current_orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'

UNION ALL

SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, 'ARCHIVE' AS source
FROM historical_orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY order_date DESC;

-- 2. UNION: Required when combining two distinct contact lists to eliminate duplicates
SELECT email FROM customer_contacts
UNION
SELECT email FROM newsletter_subscribers;
breakdown: UNION ALL simply appends result sets, running in O(N + M) time with zero sorting or hash tables required.
UNION enforces distinctness across all projected columns, requiring an O(N log N) sort or hash-unique operation.
Defaulting to UNION ALL unless duplicates are strictly impossible to tolerate is a key SQL performance rule.
Column counts and data types must match positionally in both branches.
expectedOutput:
order_id | customer_id | order_date | total_amount | source
9001     | 104         | 2026-03-01 | 150.00       | ACTIVE
4002     | 104         | 2025-12-20 | 220.00       | ARCHIVE

title: Set Operations: EXCEPT / MINUS for Change Data Capture (CDC) Set Comparison
whatThisCodeCovers: Identifies rows that exist in the staging dataset but are completely absent from the production warehouse using the EXCEPT (MINUS) relational operator.

title: Multi-Metric Aggregation with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX

title: Conditional Aggregation with CASE for Dynamic Column Pivot
whatThisCodeCovers: Pivots categorical row data into discrete columnar summaries using SUM(CASE ...) or COUNT(CASE ...) in standard ANSI SQL.
code:
-- Pivot order statuses into distinct status columns per fiscal year
SELECT 
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS fiscal_year,
    COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'CANCELLED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'REFUNDED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS refunded_orders,
    ROUND(
        100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 
        2
    ) AS completion_rate_pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)
ORDER BY fiscal_year DESC;
breakdown: CASE WHEN inside an aggregate function acts as an inline filter per row before aggregation.
SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) accurately tallies matching occurrences in a single table pass.
Avoids multiple separate queries or expensive self-joins to achieve column pivoting.
100% compliant across all standard ANSI SQL databases.
expectedOutput:
fiscal_year | total_orders | completed_orders | cancelled_orders | refunded_orders | completion_rate_pct

title: Filtering Grouped Sets: WHERE vs HAVING Execution Order
whatThisCodeCovers: Demonstrates how pre-aggregation row filtering in WHERE dramatically reduces workload before post-aggregation group filtering in HAVING.
code:
-- Find high-volume corporate clients with over 5 completed enterprise purchases
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.company_name,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS qualified_orders,
    SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spend
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o 
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_status = 'COMPLETED'     -- Step 1: Pre-aggregation filter (discards pending/cancelled early)
  AND o.order_date >= '2026-01-01'      -- Step 2: Eliminates historical years
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.company_name
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) >= 5          -- Step 3: Post-aggregation filter on grouped results
   AND SUM(o.total_amount) > 50000.00
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
breakdown: WHERE filters base table tuples prior to grouping, reducing the number of rows entered into the aggregation hash table.
HAVING executes after GROUP BY, filtering aggregate groupings based on group summaries.
Putting non-aggregate filters in HAVING is an anti-pattern because it forces the database to aggregate rows that could have been discarded early in WHERE.
Both clauses work together in standard SQL to isolate qualifying analytical cohorts.
expectedOutput:
customer_id | company_name        | qualified_orders | total_spend
441         | Apex Global Corp    | 12               | 145000.00
108         | Quantum Dynamics    | 7                | 82500.00

title: Advanced Multi-Dimensional Aggregation with GROUPING SETS
whatThisCodeCovers: Computes multiple levels of aggregation (by region, by product, and overall grand total) in a single unified table pass using GROUPING SETS.
code:
-- Multi-dimensional sales report: By region, by category, and grand total
SELECT 
    COALESCE(region, '[All Regions]') AS region_label,
    COALESCE(category, '[All Categories]') AS category_label,
    GROUPING(region) AS is_region_subtotal,
    GROUPING(category) AS is_category_subtotal,
    SUM(sale_amount) AS total_sales
FROM regional_sales
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
    (region, category),  -- Detail level
    (region),            -- Subtotal per region
    (category),          -- Subtotal per category
    ()                   -- Grand total across all rows
)
ORDER BY GROUPING(region), GROUPING(category), region, category;
breakdown: GROUPING SETS computes specified aggregate combinations in one query, avoiding multiple UNION ALL statements.
GROUPING(col) returns 1 if the column is aggregated out in a subtotal, and 0 if it is part of the grouping key.
COALESCE tags subtotal rows with clean human-readable labels.
Drastically reduces I/O by scanning the underlying table only once.
expectedOutput:
region_label  | category_label  | is_region_subtotal | is_category_subtotal | total_sales
East          | Hardware        | 0                  | 0                    | 45000.00
East          | Software        | 0                  | 0                    | 30000.00
East          | [All Categories]| 0                  | 1                    | 75000.00
[All Regions] | [All Categories]| 1                  | 1                    | 220000.00

title: Safe Ratio Calculations Defending Against Division-by-Zero (NULLIF)
whatThisCodeCovers: Defends mission-critical financial and analytical queries against fatal division-by-zero database errors using NULLIF and COALESCE.
code:
-- Calculating conversion rates and click-through rates safely
SELECT 
    campaign_id,
    impressions,
    clicks,
    conversions,
    -- NULLIF returns NULL if clicks == 0, preventing division by zero crash
    ROUND(
        COALESCE(100.0 * clicks / NULLIF(impressions, 0), 0.0), 
        2
    ) AS ctr_pct,
    ROUND(
        COALESCE(100.0 * conversions / NULLIF(clicks, 0), 0.0), 
        2
    ) AS conversion_pct
FROM ad_campaign_stats;
breakdown: Dividing any number by 0 in SQL raises a fatal runtime exception (e.g., 'division by zero') terminating the query.
NULLIF(col, 0) transforms 0 into NULL. In SQL, any number divided by NULL yields NULL.
COALESCE(..., 0.0) captures the resulting NULL and converts it safely into 0.0 for UI display.
Standard bulletproof pattern for KPI calculations in reporting engines.

campaign_id | impressions | clicks | conversions | ctr_pct | conversion_pct
CMP-101     | 50000       | 1200   | 180         | 2.40    | 15.00
CMP-102     | 0           | 0      | 0           | 0.00    | 0.00
CMP-103     | 1000        | 0      | 0           | 0.00    | 0.00

title: Three-Valued Logic Defense in Aggregates and Filtering
whatThisCodeCovers: Demonstrates how SQL three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN) handles NULLs and how to safely compute boolean flag distributions.
code:
-- Safe handling of tri-state flags: Verified, Unverified, and Unknown/Pending
SELECT 
    COALESCE(is_email_verified, FALSE) AS verified_state,
    COUNT(*) AS total_users,
    SUM(CASE WHEN is_email_verified IS TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS strictly_true_count,
    SUM(CASE WHEN is_email_verified IS NOT TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS not_true_count
FROM users
GROUP BY COALESCE(is_email_verified, FALSE);

-- Query showing why WHERE flag <> TRUE misses NULL rows:
-- Correct way to match all unverified users including NULL:
SELECT user_id, email, is_email_verified
FROM users
WHERE is_email_verified IS NOT TRUE;
breakdown: In SQL, comparing NULL = TRUE or NULL <> TRUE evaluates to UNKNOWN, which WHERE clauses reject.
IS NOT TRUE evaluates to TRUE for both FALSE and NULL rows.
COALESCE(is_email_verified, FALSE) normalizes 3VL down to 2-valued boolean logic for reliable GROUP BY buckets.
Essential for preventing silent record exclusion bugs in user authentication and security filters.
expectedOutput:
verified_state | total_users | strictly_true_count | not_true_count
false          | 320         | 0                   | 320
true           | 880         | 880                 | 0

title: String Aggregation Pattern with GROUP_CONCAT / LISTAGG
whatThisCodeCovers: Aggregates child string values into a single delimited list per parent row across SQL dialects.
code:
-- Standard SQL aggregation of assigned tags per article
-- In ANSI SQL: LISTAGG(tag_name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY tag_name)
-- In PostgreSQL: STRING_AGG(tag_name, ', ' ORDER BY tag_name)
-- In MySQL: GROUP_CONCAT(tag_name ORDER BY tag_name SEPARATOR ', ')
SELECT 
    a.article_id,
    a.title,
    -- ANSI SQL Standard syntax:
    LISTAGG(t.tag_name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY t.tag_name ASC) AS tags_list
FROM articles a
LEFT OUTER JOIN article_tags at ON a.article_id = at.article_id
LEFT OUTER JOIN tags t ON at.tag_id = t.tag_id
GROUP BY a.article_id, a.title;
breakdown: LISTAGG aggregates string values from child rows into a formatted comma-delimited string.
WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...) determines deterministic sorting of items inside the concatenated string.
Eliminates the need for client applications to stitch together child collections in memory.
Standard pattern for building denormalized search documents or CSV export feeds.
expectedOutput:
article_id | title                   | tags_list
101        | Relational Algebra 101 | Database, Theory, Tutorials
102        | Advanced SQL Windowing | Analytics, Data Warehousing, SQL

title: Distinct Cardinality Counting Across Grouped Dimensions
whatThisCodeCovers: Calculates true unique customer reach and distinct transaction days per store without double counting multiple purchases per customer.
code:
-- Unique customer engagement and shopping frequency per store
SELECT 
    store_id,
    COUNT(order_id) AS total_orders_placed,
    COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers_reached,
    COUNT(DISTINCT order_date) AS active_business_days,
    ROUND(
        1.0 * COUNT(order_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id), 0),

title: Month-Over-Month Growth & Velocity Calculation with LAG()

-- Month-over-month MRR growth and percentage velocity

    SELECT 
        billing_month,
        SUM(mrr_amount) AS total_mrr
    FROM subscription_ledger
    GROUP BY billing_month
)
SELECT 
    billing_month,
    total_mrr,
    LAG(total_mrr, 1) OVER (ORDER BY billing_month) AS prev_month_mrr,

    event_time,
    event_name,

        ORDER BY event_time ASC

title: Cycle Detection and Loop Termination in Graph Traversal
whatThisCodeCovers: Prevents infinite loops and stack overflow crashes during recursive graph traversal by tracking visited nodes in an array or string path.
code:
-- Traverse directed graph nodes while safely terminating if a cycle is detected
WITH RECURSIVE graph_path AS (
    -- Anchor: Starting node
    SELECT 
        source_node,
        target_node,
        CAST('/' || source_node || '/' || target_node || '/' AS VARCHAR(1000)) AS path_string,
        FALSE AS is_cycle
    FROM graph_edges
    WHERE source_node = 'A'

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive Step: Advance along edges, halting if target already exists in path
    SELECT 
        e.source_node,
        e.target_node,
        CAST(gp.path_string || e.target_node || '/' AS VARCHAR(1000)),
        CASE 
            WHEN gp.path_string LIKE '%/' || e.target_node || '/%' THEN TRUE 
            ELSE FALSE 
        END
    FROM graph_edges e
    INNER JOIN graph_path gp 
        ON e.source_node = gp.target_node
    WHERE NOT gp.is_cycle -- Halt branch if cycle was detected in previous step
      AND gp.path_string NOT LIKE '%/' || e.target_node || '/%' -- Prevent expanding cycle node
)
SELECT 
    source_node,
    target_node,
    path_string,
    is_cycle
FROM graph_path;
breakdown: Graphs with cycles (e.g. A -> B -> C -> A) cause naive recursive CTEs to loop infinitely until system memory or max-recursion limits trigger.
Maintains a path_string breadcrumb recording every traversed node delimiter: '/A/B/'.
Tests `path_string NOT LIKE '%/' || target || '/%'` to terminate recursion before re-visiting an already encountered vertex.
Safely isolates circular dependencies without bringing down database workers.
expectedOutput:
source_node | target_node | path_string    | is_cycle
A           | B           | /A/B/          | false
B           | C           | /A/B/C/        | false
C           | D           | /A/B/C/D/      | false

-- Find flight routes between SFO and JFK with at most 2 layovers
WITH RECURSIVE flight_search AS (
    -- Anchor: Direct departures from SFO
    SELECT 
        origin,
        destination,
        cost,
        1 AS num_hops,
        CAST(origin || ' -> ' || destination AS VARCHAR(500)) AS itinerary
    FROM flight_legs
    WHERE origin = 'SFO'

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive Member: Connect connecting flights
    SELECT 
        fs.origin,
        fl.destination,
        fs.cost + fl.cost,
        fs.num_hops + 1,
        CAST(fs.itinerary || ' -> ' || fl.destination AS VARCHAR(500))
    FROM flight_search fs
    INNER JOIN flight_legs fl 
        ON fs.destination = fl.origin
    WHERE fs.num_hops < 3 -- Maximum 2 layovers (3 hops)
      AND fs.destination <> 'JFK' -- Stop traversing if destination reached
)
SELECT 
    itinerary,
    num_hops,
    cost
FROM flight_search
WHERE destination = 'JFK'
ORDER BY cost ASC, num_hops ASC;

code:
-- Calculate 12-month loan amortization schedule for a $10,000 loan at 1% monthly interest
WITH RECURSIVE amortization AS (
    -- Anchor: Month 0 (Starting loan balance)
    SELECT 
        0 AS month_num,
        CAST(10000.00 AS NUMERIC(12,2)) AS remaining_balance,
        CAST(0.00 AS NUMERIC(12,2)) AS interest_paid,
        CAST(0.00 AS NUMERIC(12,2)) AS principal_paid
    
    UNION ALL
    
    -- Recursive Step: Advance month by month with $888.49 fixed payment
    SELECT 
        a.month_num + 1,
        CAST(
            a.remaining_balance + (a.remaining_balance * 0.01) - 888.49 
            AS NUMERIC(12,2)
        ),
        CAST(a.remaining_balance * 0.01 AS NUMERIC(12,2)),
        CAST(888.49 - (a.remaining_balance * 0.01) AS NUMERIC(12,2))
    FROM amortization a
    WHERE a.month_num < 12
)
SELECT 
    month_num,
    remaining_balance,
    interest_paid,
    principal_paid
FROM amortization
WHERE month_num > 0
ORDER BY month_num;
breakdown: Emulates imperative looping directly within declarative SQL.
Each iterative step receives the previous month's remaining balance, applies interest, deducts payment, and passes state to the next row.
Terminates deterministically when month_num reaches 12.
Computes complete amortization schedules without pulling data out to Python or Excel.
expectedOutput:
month_num | remaining_balance | interest_paid | principal_paid
1         | 9211.51           | 100.00        | 788.49
2         | 8415.14           | 92.12         | 796.37
12        | 0.00              | 8.80          | 879.69

title: Querying Closure Tables for High-Speed Arbitrary Depth Subtree Lookups
whatThisCodeCovers: Demonstrates querying a relational Closure Table (ancestor, descendant, depth) to fetch an entire subtree instantaneously in O(1) joins without recursive overhead.
code:
-- Retrieve all descendants under 'Engineering' (dept_id = 10) at any depth
SELECT 
    d.department_id,
    d.department_name,
    c.depth
FROM department_closure c
INNER JOIN departments d 
    ON c.descendant_id = d.department_id
WHERE c.ancestor_id = 10
ORDER BY c.depth ASC, d.department_name ASC;
breakdown: The closure table pre-stores every ancestor-descendant pair along with the path length (depth).
Eliminates the CPU cost of recursive CTEs during high-frequency read operations.
Fetching an entire subtree of 10,000 nodes requires a simple indexed equi-join on ancestor_id.
A classic relational design trade-off: slight write amplification on insert in exchange for lightning-fast reads.
expectedOutput:
department_id | department_name       | depth
10            | Engineering           | 0
12            | Frontend Core         | 1
13            | Backend Platform      | 1
24            | Database Engineering  | 2

title: Recursive Number Series Generation for Missing Sequence Gap Detection
whatThisCodeCovers: Finds missing invoice numbers in a sequential sequence to detect deleted records or fraud using a recursive numbers tally CTE.
code:
-- Find missing invoice numbers in the range 1001 to 1010
WITH RECURSIVE expected_numbers AS (
    SELECT 1001 AS invoice_num
    UNION ALL
    SELECT invoice_num + 1 
    FROM expected_numbers 
    WHERE invoice_num < 1010
)
SELECT 
    en.invoice_num AS missing_invoice_number
FROM expected_numbers en
LEFT OUTER JOIN invoices inv 
    ON en.invoice_num = inv.invoice_number
WHERE inv.invoice_number IS NULL;
breakdown: expected_numbers generates the unbroken sequence from MIN to MAX integer bounds.
LEFT OUTER JOIN ... WHERE inv.invoice_number IS NULL isolates missing values.
Essential compliance check for legally required consecutive document number sequences (invoices, checks, receipts).
Identifies missing rows in seconds without external procedural scripts.
expectedOutput:
missing_invoice_number
1004
1007

title: Keyset Cursor Pagination on Composite Unique Keys
whatThisCodeCovers: Replaces slow, skipping-prone OFFSET pagination with deterministic, constant-time O(1) keyset (cursor) pagination using row comparison predicates.
code:
-- Fetch page 2 of 20 items where the last seen item had (created_at = '2026-03-01 14:00:00', order_id = 4590)
SELECT 
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    created_at,
    total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, order_id) < ('2026-03-01 14:00:00', 4590)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Equivalent standard expansion if database lacks tuple comparison:
-- WHERE created_at < '2026-03-01 14:00:00' 
--    OR (created_at = '2026-03-01 14:00:00' AND order_id < 4590)
breakdown: OFFSET 10000 forces the database to read, sort, and discard 10,000 physical rows before returning results (O(N) cost).
Keyset pagination seeks directly to the index position following the last seen cursor tuple in O(log N) time.
Pairing created_at with the primary key order_id ensures deterministic ordering even when timestamps collide.
Completely eliminates pagination drift when new items are inserted concurrently.

title: Batch Chunked Data Archival & Deletion Loop
whatThisCodeCovers: Purges millions of expired records safely in small bounded chunks of 5,000 rows to prevent table lock escalation, transaction log exhaustion, and replication lag.
code:
-- Purge expired audit logs in bounded chunks of 5,000 rows (run repeatedly in a script until rows_affected == 0)
DELETE FROM audit_logs
WHERE log_id IN (
    SELECT log_id
    FROM audit_logs
    WHERE log_timestamp < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90' DAY
    ORDER BY log_id ASC
    LIMIT 5000
);
breakdown: A raw 'DELETE FROM audit_logs WHERE log_timestamp < ...' on 50 million rows creates a massive lock, explodes the undo/redo log, and stalls queries.
Bounding deletes to 5,000 rows per transaction releases row locks frequently, allowing concurrent business writes to proceed.
Sorting by primary key log_id ASC prevents deadlocks between concurrent archival jobs.
Applications execute this statement in a loop until row count affected is 0.
expectedOutput: Query executed successfully. 5000 rows deleted. (Duration: 42ms)

title: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) with Version Stamp
whatThisCodeCovers: Prevents lost updates in concurrent environments by asserting that the row version stamp has not changed between reading and updating.
code:
-- Thread A and Thread B read customer with version = 4
-- Thread A executes update:
UPDATE customer_accounts
SET 
    account_balance = account_balance - 50.00,
    version = version + 1,
    updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE account_id = 'ACC-1001'
  AND version = 4; -- Assert version matches what was read

-- Application checks affected row count:
-- If affected_rows == 1: Success.
-- If affected_rows == 0: Concurrent update conflict! Roll back and retry with refreshed state.
breakdown: Avoids heavy database pessimistic locks (like SELECT FOR UPDATE) across long client interaction times.
The version predicate acts as an atomic compare-and-swap (CAS) check.
If a concurrent user updated the account first, the version is already 5, so WHERE version = 4 matches 0 rows.
The client detects zero affected rows and safely prompts the user or retries without corrupting balance.
expectedOutput: UPDATE 1 (Success: row balance decremented, version bumped from 4 to 5)

title: Parameterized Defense Against SQL Injection Attacks
whatThisCodeCovers: Contrasts catastrophic dynamic string concatenation with parameterized prepared statements across relational SQL drivers.
code:
-- 1. VULNERABLE ANTI-PATTERN: String concatenation (Never do this!)
-- Input payload: user_input = "' OR '1'='1"
-- Query executed: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1' AND is_active = TRUE;
-- Result: Leaks all accounts, bypassing authentication!

-- 2. SECURE PRODUCTION PATTERN: Parameterized Query
-- In PostgreSQL: $1, $2
-- In MySQL/SQLite: ?
-- In SQL Server/Oracle: @p1 or :p1
SELECT user_id, full_name, email, password_hash
FROM users
WHERE email = $1 
  AND is_active = TRUE;
breakdown: Dynamic string concatenation treats user input as executable SQL code, enabling malicious query injection.
Parameterized queries separate SQL structure from data: parameters are sent in a separate protocol packet after compilation.
The database parser treats parameter values strictly as literal values, never as syntax tokens or operators.
Additionally enables query execution plan reuse, speeding up high-frequency transactional lookups.
expectedOutput:
user_id | full_name | email            | password_hash
42      | Alice     | alice@target.com | $2b$12$e8Y...

title: Updatable SQL View with WITH CHECK OPTION Security Guard
whatThisCodeCovers: Creates an updatable security view that restricts tenant updates to their own organization and uses WITH CHECK OPTION to prevent privilege leakage.
code:
-- 1. Create updatable view for EMEA sales team
CREATE VIEW emea_sales_view AS
SELECT 
    sale_id,
    sales_rep_id,
    region,
    deal_value,
    status
FROM sales_opportunities
WHERE region = 'EMEA'
WITH CHECK OPTION;

-- 2. Legitimate update:
UPDATE emea_sales_view 
SET deal_value = deal_value * 1.10
WHERE sale_id = 501;

-- 3. Unauthorized attempt to hijack record into another region (BLOCKED!):
-- UPDATE emea_sales_view SET region = 'NORTH_AMERICA' WHERE sale_id = 501;
-- ERROR: new row violates WITH CHECK OPTION for view "emea_sales_view"
breakdown: Standard views with simple 1-to-1 projections without aggregates are natively updatable.
Without 'WITH CHECK OPTION', a user could UPDATE a row to change its region to 'NORTH_AMERICA', causing the row to disappear from their view and bypass boundaries.
WITH CHECK OPTION forces every INSERT and UPDATE through the view to satisfy the view's WHERE predicate.
Provides robust database-enforced row isolation for specific database users or roles.
expectedOutput: View emea_sales_view created. Updates strictly enforced against region = 'EMEA'.

title: SARGable vs Non-SARGable Range Predicates on Timestamps
whatThisCodeCovers: Fixes a notorious query performance disaster by refactoring a function-wrapped date filter into an index-friendly SARGable range predicate.
code:
-- 1. NON-SARGABLE ANTI-PATTERN: Function on column kills index seek!
-- The database must execute DATE() on every single row in the table (Full Table Scan)
SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE CAST(order_date AS DATE) = '2026-03-01';

-- 2. SARGABLE HIGH-PERFORMANCE REFACTOR: Leaves column bare!
-- Executes an instantaneous B-Tree Range Seek on the index (order_date)
SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-03-01 00:00:00'
  AND order_date < '2026-03-02 00:00:00';
breakdown: Wrapping indexed columns in functions (CAST, YEAR, UPPER, ROUND) hides the values from the B-Tree index structure.
A bare column compared against evaluated constant boundaries is SARGable, enabling O(log N) index seeks.
The half-open interval [2026-03-01, 2026-03-02) accurately captures all millisecond/microsecond variations without BETWEEN edge bugs.
Can improve query latency from 12 seconds to 2 milliseconds on large tables.

title: Row-Level Locking Patterns: SELECT FOR UPDATE vs Share Locks
whatThisCodeCovers: Acquires an exclusive row lock using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE within a transaction to safely deduct inventory without double allocation.
breakdown: SELECT FOR UPDATE places an exclusive row-level lock on the selected row until the transaction commits or aborts.
Other concurrent transactions attempting to read with FOR UPDATE on the same row will wait until the lock is released.
Prevents flash sale over-selling race conditions where two threads read stock = 1 simultaneously and both decrement.
Always ensure transactions with FOR UPDATE are kept minimal and fast to prevent lock queues.
expectedOutput: COMMIT completed. Inventory deducted safely without race conditions.

title: Multi-Table Transaction with Rollback and Savepoints
whatThisCodeCovers: Demonstrates transaction management with partial rollback to a SAVEPOINT, allowing non-critical operations to fail without aborting the main transaction.
breakdown: BEGIN TRANSACTION initiates an atomic block guaranteeing all-or-nothing execution.
SAVEPOINT marks an intermediate milestone within the transaction.
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes changes made after the savepoint without discarding the preceding updates.
COMMIT persists all active changes durably to disk.
expectedOutput: Transaction committed successfully. Primary funds transfer guaranteed.

title: Least Privilege Security: Granting Granular Table and Column Permissions
whatThisCodeCovers: Enforces the principle of least privilege by granting specific read/write permissions to custom application roles and masking sensitive columns.
breakdown: Never connect production applications using the superuser ('postgres' or 'root') account.
GRANT SELECT (col1, col2) restricts the role from projecting sensitive columns like ssn or password_hash.
Attempting 'SELECT ssn FROM customers' using reporting_readonly_user raises an immediate SQL permission denied error.
Revoking defaults from PUBLIC ensures defense-in-depth across the entire schema.
expectedOutput: Roles and granular permissions configured. Sensitive fields masked from reporting user.

title: Schema Evolution: Adding Non-Null Columns with Defaults Without Locking
whatThisCodeCovers: Analyzes modern ANSI and relational patterns for non-blocking DDL migrations when adding NOT NULL columns with default values to massive tables.
code:
-- Modern Zero-Downtime Migration Pattern:
-- In modern SQL engines, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT and NOT NULL is a metadata-only change (O(1)).
-- In legacy databases, breaking it into phased steps prevents full-table rewrite:

-- Step 1: Add column as nullable (instantaneous metadata update)
ALTER TABLE user_accounts 
ADD COLUMN is_mfa_enabled BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE;

-- Step 2: Backfill existing rows in bounded batches (if legacy engine did not backfill in metadata)
-- UPDATE user_accounts SET is_mfa_enabled = FALSE WHERE is_mfa_enabled IS NULL;

-- Step 3: Add NOT NULL constraint once existing rows are compliant
ALTER TABLE user_accounts 
ALTER COLUMN is_mfa_enabled SET NOT NULL;
breakdown: In older database engines, ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT ... NOT NULL locked the entire table while rewriting every row on disk.
Modern relational engines (PostgreSQL 11+, modern MySQL/SQL Server) optimize constant defaults as fast metadata updates.
Breaking large migrations into nullable addition, batch backfilling, and constraint enforcement prevents production table deadlocks.
Fundamental standard practice for zero-downtime continuous deployment pipelines.
expectedOutput: ALTER TABLE completed. Column added without table rewrite lock.
